stories.title: DeMarvion Overshown didn't know inactive players couldn't celebrate on the field
stories.summary: The Cowboys had 14 accepted penalties for 153 yards in the 27-23 win over the Colts.
stories.detailText: The Cowboys had 14 accepted penalties for 153 yards in the 27-23 win over the Colts. One of them was called unacceptable and undisciplined by Cowboys executive vice president Stephen Jones. Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown, who was inactive and dressed in street clothes, came onto the field to celebrate after Quinnen Williams forced a Jonathan Taylor fumble that Shemar James returned to the Dallas 30. Overshown was penalized 15 yards, with referee Clay Martin saying, "After the play, unsportsmanlike conduct by Dallas. We have non-uniformed player in blue sweats and a stocking cap come onto the field to celebrate. That's a 15-yard penalty." Overshown apologized to head coach Brian Schottenheimer and his teammates. “At the end of the day, I talked to Schotty about it," Overshown said Thursday, via Calvin Watkins of the Dallas Morning News . "I apologized about it. It was definitely in the moment, but earlier I had said that as a defense, we're going to start celebrating more, getting takeaways. And I was just caught in the moment. So you can laugh at it now, because we won the game, but in the moment, fourth quarter, tied ball game or close ball game, you don't want a 15-yard penalty from a guy, especially that's not even playing. So that's a lesson learned.” Overshown said he didn't know the rule until linebacker Dee Winters started yelling at him, which should prompt questions about why Overshown didn't know the rule. But he defended Schottenheimer and said he accepted his "butt chewing." “It’s not an indictment on Schotty. It’s on me as a player. I own it,” he said.

stories.title: Throwback Thursday: The time Tony Gonzalez was almost traded
stories.summary: Kansas City’s first All-World tight end was almost dealt midseason before he actually left town.
stories.detailText: With the NFL Trade Deadline passing this week, it’s a good time to remember an era when the Kansas City Chiefs were more often sellers than buyers at this time of year. We ask @JayGlazer about the craziest trade that never happened. 👀 pic.twitter.com/Z14VL98lUR — Dan Patrick Show (@dpshow) November 11, 2026 Wednesday morning, on “The Dan Patrick Show,” Fox Sports NFL Insider shared a story about former Chiefs tight end Tony Gonzalez nearly being traded midseason. He reminisced about negotiations between Kansas City and two franchises: the Philadelphia Eagles , led by head coach Andy Reid, and the Green Bay Packers , led by Mike McCarthy. “Tony Gonzalez wants to get traded from the Chiefs, right?” Glazer remembered. “At the time, Carl Peterson was the GM; he had two deals: one with the Eagles and one with the Packers. Andy Reid and the Eagles were offered a [third-round pick] and LJ Smith, their tight end, and the Packers were offered a three and whoever their tight end was.” Glazer is most likely referring to the 2008 season, a lost year in Kansas City that featured a 2-14 record. The year before, the Chiefs went 4-12. The Packers tight end he was likely referring to was Donald Lee, but Green Bay also had 21-year-old Jermichael Finley on the 2008 team. “This is Tony: he talked to the Chiefs. He wanted to finish his career on a contender,” Glazer recalled. “He wanted to go somewhere else, and they agreed. So they’re really going back and forth, and it’s really up to him.” “Maybe 20 minutes before, Carl Peterson changes it from a three to a two, and there just wasn’t enough time to do it, right? I got a text from Andy Reid like, ‘I knew this wasn’t going to happen.’ I got a text from McCarthy: furious.” Glazer told Patrick that Gonzalez lost it when hearing that the trade didn’t go through. He was ready to put the Chiefs on blast for not letting him leave town: “Get your pen out!” “He wanted to do a story that there was no way we could ever publish in the history of life,” Glazer said. “I never do stories where someone is just emotional… he was like ‘I’m never playing!‘” “He calmed down — might’ve taken a couple of days off — and went out and finished with Kansas City,” Glazer finished. “Eventually, him and Scott Pioli and Todd Haley were horrible, and they traded him to Atlanta.” Gonzalez was traded to the Atlanta Falcons the following spring in 2009, and finally won a playoff game in the Divisional Round of the 2012 season. If the trade had gone through with Green Bay, Tony G could’ve had his Super Bowl ring with the 2010 Packers and quarterback Aaron Rodgers. Too bad.

teamStories.summary: — The change came quickly Tuesday, but it was not unexpected when the
teamStories.detailText: LAS VEGAS -- — The change came quickly Tuesday , but it was not unexpected when the Las Vegas Raiders shipped quarterback Kirk Cousins to Minnesota and installed rookie Fernando Mendoza as their starter . As the top draft pick, Mendoza taking over has been anticipated for months by Raiders fans and was a topic of discussion throughout the NFL. And what a time to make his debut, going against a Seattle Seahawks defense on Sunday that allows a league-low 244.2 yards per game and puts even the league's top quarterbacks in uncomfortable situations. “Every week in the NFL is tough, and this is the best defense in the NFL,” Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said. “(Mendoza's) got to go do his job and not worry about a whole lot else.” Kubiak knows all about the Seahawks' defense, going against it in practice last season as Seattle's offensive coordinator . He spent just the one season with Seattle, but his offense led by quarterback Sam Darnold and running back Kenneth Walker III paired with coach Mike Macdonald's Dark Side defense led to the organization's second Super Bowl championship. That was a team more ready to win than Las Vegas, which is showing signs of progress, having already surpassed its three wins from last season. The Raiders average 26.4 points per game, eighth in the NFL, after reaching that number just once in 2025. “They’re building it around the people that they have and they’re doing it at a high level,” Macdonald said. “I respect how they operate, obviously, and they have great people and good players. They’re moving the ball and putting up a lot of points.” Macdonald and his staff don't have much video on Mendoza, who has made just one appearance. Mendoza completed 6 of 8 passes for 48 yards late in a blowout loss to New England. There is a lot of pressure on Mendoza, who has been in the spotlight since winning the Heisman Trophy last season and leading Indiana to the national championship. He has acknowledged a big learning curve, and the Raiders brought Mendoza along slowly while Cousins ran the offense. Word from the Raiders' locker room was Mendoza made the most of that time and put together some outstanding practices in recent weeks. “Sometimes coach Sully (QBs coach Mike Sullivan) will reference back to ‘Spring Fernando,’” Mendoza said. “I don’t want to talk about myself in the third person, but it just shows how much improvement there’s been. I’m a lot more confident as a quarterback, and I feel more developed.” Need to know Seattle (5-4) at Las Vegas (4-5). When/where to watch: Sunday, 4:05 p.m. EST, CBS. Latest odds: Seahawks by 6 1/2. Against the spread: Seahawks 3-4-2; Raiders 6-3. Last week: Seahawks beat the Cardinals 17-3; Raiders lost to the 49ers 38-17. Last meeting: Raiders won 40-34 in overtime on Nov. 27, 2022, in Seattle. Series record: Raiders lead 29-25. Matchup to watch Mendoza vs. Seahawks S Nick Emmanwori . Mendoza will have to be aware of the aggressive Emmanwori, who has blitzed on 54 plays, according to the NFL's Next Gen Stats. That is the most among defensive backs. Emmanwori blitzed 65 times all of last season, and his 17 quarterback pressures match his total from last year. Stats and stuff — The Seahawks have not allowed a 100-yard rusher in 38 consecutive games, including playoffs. Las Vegas a team has eclipsed 100 yards rushing just twice this season and not since Week 3 at New Orleans. — Seattle's Drew Lock is the only quarterback with 75 or more passes and no interceptions. He also has thrown five touchdown passes in three games and has a 116.0 QB rating. Lock is filling in for starter Sam Darnold, who is out for the second week in a row because of a quadriceps injury. — The Seahawks' 16-4 road record since 2024 is the league's best. — This is the Seahawks' first regular-season game in Las Vegas since the Raiders moved there in 2020. — Mendoza will become the fifth top overall draft pick at quarterback to made his first start in Week 10 or later in the common draft era, according to Next Gen Stats. The other four — Jared Goff in 2016, JaMarcus Russell in 2007, Eli Manning in 2004 and Vinny Testaverde in 1987 — lost their debut starts. — Kubiak is the seventh to win a Super Bowl as a coordinator and then meet that team the following season as the opponent's head coach. Howard Schnellenberger, in 1972 against Miami, is the only coach to win in such a scenario. — Brock Bowers is the fastest tight end to reach 2,500 receiving yards, getting there in 36 games. That's one fewer than Kellen Winslow. — The Raiders are the only team to not give up a sack on a blitz. — Raiders linebackers Nakobe Dean and Quay Walker have combined for 170 tackles, the most of any NFL duo. ------ See AP’s full NFL coverage here

teamStories.title: Is there a quick fix to the Las Vegas Raiders’ defensive woes?
teamStories.summary: Ranking dead last in points, yards allowed, and total rushing yards yielded a triple threat of woes for Rob Leonard
teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images Immediately after his football team lost to the San Francisco 49ers 38-17 this past Sunday, Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak was naturally asked about potential changes to a defense that’s now given up 30 or more points in six straight games. “We will look at the film, and we will make our decisions when we have cooler heads,” the rookie head coach said combating the need to make any rash decisions. Cooler heads prevailed and on Monday, Kubiak expressed confidence in his chosen rookie defensive coordinator Rob Leonard and emphatically shut the door on any changes in that regard. “No, I don’t. In fact, I see us doing the things we said we were going to do better. Stand behind Rob (Leonard). Stand behind our defensive staff. Stand behind our players,” Kubiak said during his Monday media availability. “And I think the world wants someone’s head on a platter every time things don’t go right. But the way that I see it is that we brought people here for a reason, to get a job done and develop players for the long haul, and that’s where we’re going.” Kubiak’s decision to stand behind Leonard, the defensive staff, and the players on that side of the ball likely draws mixed feelings from Raider Nation. After all, Las Vegas tied a modern-era NFL record of six-straight games allowing 30 or more points and team is ranked dead-last out of the 32 teams in: Points allowed (268), yards allowed (3,469), rushing yards yielded (1,361), and first downs given up (208). #Raiders HC Klint Kubiak said they won’t be making changes to their defensive staff “I’m standing behind Rob, I’m standing behind our defensive staff, I’m standing behind our players. I think the world wants someone’s head on a platter every time things don’t go right…” Said… pic.twitter.com/nSlyXHTo06 — Jesse Merrick – Silver & Black Sports Network (@JesseSBSN) November 9, 2026 Being the caboose in the league in those categories isn’t a recipe for success, it’s a blueprint in ineptitude. Which beckons a question: Is there a quick fix to the Silver & Black’s defensive woes? An emphatic no, is the answer. Even if Kubiak decided to part ways with Leonard nine games into his initial tenure as an NFL defensive coordinator, the underlying issues remain — no matter who is promoted to interim play caller status. The cauldron of misery is a mix of both schematic and roster issues and it continues to simmer in a piping hot boil. There’s a glaring lack of talent — particularly in the trenches at defensive tackle — and no matter what play calls Leonard deploys to make up for that — more man coverage and blitzing — the results are there for everyone to see. The Raiders are gashed by the run and are habitually beaten through the air. Now it isn’t all bad. Leonard’s group showed sharper execution and focus in the second half in both Weeks 8 and 9 by rising to the occasion against the New York Jets and the San Francisco 49ers this past Sunday. But the moments of efficiency are too fleeting. And this shouldn’t be a surprise for folk who watched the offseason. Yes, the Raiders are in rebuild mode. Yes, the talent gaps weren’t going to be filled in one offseason. And yes, it’ll take the coaching staff time to truly integrate their philosophy on a roster that’s going through natural turnover during this early phase of the Kubiak era. But the expected growing pains shouldn’t absolve folk of criticism — from Kubiak, Leonard, and general manager John Spytek and Co. The ownership of a historically woeful defense is a beast of burden that multiple Raiders share. After the Raiders' 38-17 loss to the 49ers, Quay Walker talked about how slow starts on defense are a big reason they have allowed 30+ points for the sixth straight week. pic.twitter.com/oKwV5tZblS — Raider Nation Radio (@RNR920AM) November 9, 2026 Listening to linebacker Quay Walker above is encouraging. And it’s true all 11 defenders need to be on the same page on the field — ditto for the coaches and other defenders on the sideline. Unfortunately for the Walker — the 26-year-old free agent catch who inked a three-year, $40.5 million deal with the Raiders in the offseason — he’s a culprit of not playing as one, communicating, or executing properly in a glaring play against the Niners that left running back Christian McCaffrey wide open for a walk-in touchdown pass. It was a sequence that saw both defensive tackles Tonka Hemingway and Adam Butler dropping into zone coverage, with the former the “closest” defender to CMC. “It was. Yeah, we did not peel on the halfback,” Kubiak said of the play in particular , noting that play was a situation where another player just had an execution issue. “That was not those guys’ (Hemingway and Butler) job, though.” That defender is most likely Walker who should’ve have peeled back to cover McCaffrey instead of moving towards San Francisco quarterback Brock Purdy. But amongst the myriad of lowlights, there were highlights from Leonard’s Raiders defense in Week 9. Edge rusher Maxx Crosby dropped Purdy for his fourth sack of the season just before halftime. The play showcases what is possible when all three levels of Las Vegas defense is on point — rush, second level, and backend coverage. As does the interception by rookie safety Treydan Stukes early in the third quarter. Kubiak waxes poetic about the culture and standard that he’s continuing to instill upon his Raiders. Former starting quarterback Kirk Cousins — who was traded to the Minnesota Vikings before the NFL trade deadline this past Tuesday for a 2027 third-round pick — helped foster the high-level of play that’s expected to permeate throughout the Raiders’ building. One can argue keeping Leonard in place creates a lack of accountability as the play under the defensive coordinator falls well below what Kubiak expects from his football team. Maxx Crosby with the SACK 😤 LVvsSF on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/xvZEgltKmI — NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026 On the other hand, Kubiak backing Leonard avoids the toxicity of canning a first-time defensive boss that’s growing into the role much like the head coach who chose him. Publicly backing his much-maligned defensive play caller showcases the head coach’s ability to back an assistant threw serious growing pains. And that’s what Kubiak will do through the rest of the 2026 campaign. Live with his choice and see if Leonard rises to the occasion or wilts under the pressure. We don’t know what’s being said behind closed doors, perhaps Leonard is on the receiving end of some harsh criticism from Kubiak that never leaves Raiders’ HQ? Leonard is given a chance to work through the schematic issues. The talent and depth limitations are an offseason item — at the earliest. Las Vegas could dig into the practice squad and elevate 2026 seventh-round pick Brandon Cleveland to the active roster at some point to see if the 6-foot-4 and 315-pound 22-year old can bolster the defensive tackle position, for instance. But until free agency next March and the 2027 NFL Draft a month later — shoot even a full offseason where Kubiak can scour potential replacements for Leonard — true reinforcements are far beyond the horizon. In the meantime, a focus on fundamentals with defenders being in position to make plays, execution, and the continued grind is what’s there for Leonard and Kubiak. Las Vegas still ranks in the upper echelon in terms of takeaways with 14 — good for sixth best in the NFL. And that was the difference maker last Sunday when the 49ers forced turnovers to thwart the Raiders’ offensive attack. Leonard has his reprieve from Kubiak. We’ll see if he can become the coach the head coach believes he can be or if he continues to fumble a golden opportunity away.
